title: Peso firms as oil prices ease
teaser: NFA palay buying falls short, LPG may dip again in December, Sachet drop-off at select supermarkets

sections.headline: Peso firms as oil prices ease
sections.body: The peso closed stronger against the US dollar on Wednesday, its second straight day of gains, as global oil prices kept falling. The Philippines buys most of its fuel abroad, so cheaper crude means the country needs fewer dollars for imports, and that supports the peso. RCBC chief economist Michael Ricafort said lower oil, now near three-month lows, could help ease inflation, meaning slower price increases at home. The stock market rose too: the PSEi, the main index of the biggest listed companies, gained 0.68 percent to 5,493.41, although foreign investors were still net sellers. For the family, a firmer peso helps with prices at home, but each dollar sent home converts to slightly fewer pesos. What is still unknown: a trader said the peso "might weaken ahead of a likely strong US PCE report overnight," a US inflation gauge that can move the dollar. *Manila Times Business*: [Declining oil price boosts peso; stock market nears 5,500 level](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/11/26/business/top-business/declining-oil-price-boosts-peso-stock-market-nears-5500-level/2478055)

items.text: *GMA Money* reports that Ricafort also linked the peso's nearly month-long gain to reassurance from President Marcos since October 28, 2026, after the peso breached P64 to the dollar late last month: [Philippine peso gains anew against US dollar amid global fuel price decline](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/money/economy/1010761/philippine-peso-gains-anew-against-us-dollar-amid-global-fuel-price-decline/story/)

sections.socialHook: The peso gained for a second straight day as world oil prices fell. Good for prices at home, but your dollars now stretch a little less. Here's what changed.
sections.soWhat: A stronger peso means the same dollars sent home buy slightly fewer pesos; the rate block above shows today's reference rate.

sections.headline: NFA palay buying falls short
sections.body: The National Food Authority (NFA), the agency that buys palay (unmilled rice) from farmers for the government's rice reserves, says it has bought about 175,000 metric tons this year, only 22 to 25 percent of its 790,000-MT target. Administrator Larry Lacson blamed smaller harvests: farmers used less fertilizer, which he linked to disruptions from the fighting in the Middle East, and heavy rains and the habagat hit crops. The Philippine Statistics Authority reported palay output fell 17.8% year on year in the third quarter. The NFA is aiming to buy 380,000 MT more to support the P20-per-kilo *Benteng Bigas, Meron Na!* program and its reserves, and has raised its buying price to up to P30 per kilo for clean, dry palay. Its warehouse stock covers about eight days of demand. Lacson said imported rice will not be sold in the P20 program. Still unknown: whether the November and early December harvest is enough to catch up. *BusinessWorld*: [NFA missing palay procurement target, seeking to buy additional 380,000 MT](https://bworldonline.com/economy/2026/11/25/796796/nfa-missing-palay-procurement-target-seeking-to-buy-additional-380000-mt/)

items.text: *Manila Times Business* reports that Lacson said rice imports will go to the wider retail market, leaving local harvests for the P20 program: "We still have stocks left." [NFA's palay procurement lower than target as of end-October](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/11/26/business/top-business/nfas-palay-procurement-lower-than-target-as-of-end-october/2478059)

sections.socialHook: Rice harvests are smaller this year, and the NFA has bought only about a quarter of its palay target. What it means for the P20-per-kilo rice program.
sections.soWhat: Harvests are down; if your family budgets around P20-per-kilo rice, the NFA says the program still runs on local stock for now.

sections.headline: LPG may dip again in December
sections.body: LPG, the bottled cooking gas in most Filipino kitchens, may get cheaper again in December. Republic Gas Corp. President Arnel Ty told One News that prices could slide by an additional P4 to P6 in the coming weeks as contract prices, the international benchmark prices importers pay, keep softening. He said the country's inventory is enough for 35 to 45 days, so holiday demand should not cause a shortage. Consumer fuel prices have dropped three weeks in a row, and LPG firms made P2 rollbacks, or price cuts, in early November. The Philippines imports most of its petroleum products from the Middle East, which keeps local prices sensitive to conflict there. What is not yet known: this is one industry executive's estimate, not an announced price, and this report is our only source. Separately, the Palace said no details are final on US President Donald Trump's claim that the Philippines agreed to buy all its energy and farm needs from the US. *PhilStar Business*: [LPG prices seen declining further in December](https://www.philstar.com/business/2026/11/25/2572332/lpg-prices-seen-declining-further-december)
sections.socialHook: Cooking gas may get cheaper again in December, says one LPG company head. Not official yet, but here's what to expect when you refill the tangke.
sections.soWhat: If you buy a tangke at home, a further P4 to P6 cut in December is possible but not yet announced; check the price when you refill.

sections.headline: Sachet drop-off at select supermarkets
sections.body: A small heads-up this week, not a deadline or a fee. Nestlé Philippines says it has collected more than one million used sachets since July through reverse vending machines, drop-off machines that take empty packaging, at select Robinsons Supermarket branches in Metro Manila, set up with Restore Solutions PH. If the family in Metro Manila goes through a lot of coffee or shampoo sachets, these machines are a place to bring them instead of the trash. We only have the headline and summary: which branches have machines, and whether you get anything back, is not stated. *Inquirer Business*: [Nestlé recovers 1M sachets in Metro Manila since July](https://business.inquirer.net/622850/nestle-recovers-1m-sachets-in-metro-manila-since-july)
sections.socialHook: Those empty sachets piling up at home? Some Metro Manila supermarkets now have machines that take them. A small, free habit for the family.
sections.soWhat: No cost and no deadline; families in Metro Manila can ask their Robinsons Supermarket branch if it has a sachet drop-off machine.

sections.headline: Iba pang balita

items.text: The Department of Agriculture suspended imports of poultry, pork and live animals from four countries under Department Circular No. 57 to guard against animal diseases; the summary we have does not name the countries. *Inquirer Business*: [DA suspends meat, live animal imports from 4 countries](https://business.inquirer.net/622846/da-suspends-meat-live-animal-imports-from-4-countries)

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is watching banks' lending to agriculture more closely during El Niño, with relief measures on standby for lenders hit by calamities. *Inquirer Business*: [BSP tightens watch on banks' agri loans amid El Niño losses](https://business.inquirer.net/622865/bsp-tightens-watch-on-banks-agri-loans-amid-el-nino-losses)

Under Department Circular No. 58, the DA now allows live pigs, pork and pork products from UK areas free of African swine fever, a deadly pig disease. *GMA Money*: [PH allows pork importation from ASF-free areas in UK](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/money/economy/1010824/ph-allows-pork-importation-from-asf-free-areas-in-uk/story/)

Liquor makers told a House committee that raising excise taxes, the special taxes on goods like alcohol, on ready-to-drink cocktails could push buyers toward cheaper illegal products; this is the industry's position at a hearing. *BusinessWorld*: [Liquor industry warns ready-to-drink alcohol market at risk if excise taxes raised](https://bworldonline.com/economy/2026/11/25/796863/liquor-industry-warns-ready-to-drink-alcohol-market-at-risk-if-excise-taxes-raised/)

sections.socialHook: Also this morning: a pause on meat imports from four countries, UK pork allowed back in, and a closer watch on farm loans during El Niño.
